collection: NERDC Primary 4 Basic Digital Literacy online safety
note: Original practice. Four offline role-plays and sixteen written precursors. Classroom delivery and school adoption unverified; independent academic review pending.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.prompt: Your teacher gives the class an approved reading-site bookmark. A pop-up on another page invites you to an unknown game site. Which is the better choice for the reading task, and what should you do about the invitation?
questions.answer: Use the approved bookmark for the reading task. Do not follow the unknown invitation; ask the teacher to check it.
questions.explanation: Teacher approval is for a particular learning task. It does not mean every link or advertisement on a page is safe.

markingGuide.description: Selects the approved reading bookmark.
Asks the teacher about the invitation without following it.

questions.deliveryNote: Written understanding or planning precursor. This task alone does not demonstrate actual online behaviour. Use fictional examples and no personal information.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.prompt: A classmate says a website is suitable for Primary 4 because its home page has bright colours. Give one reason this is not enough, and name someone who can help check whether it is suitable.
questions.answer: Colours do not tell us whether the content and activities are suitable. A parent or teacher can help check it.
questions.explanation: Appearance alone does not establish suitability for children.

markingGuide.description: Explains that appearance does not establish suitable content or activities.
Names a parent, teacher or other trusted adult.

questions.deliveryNote: Written understanding or planning precursor. This task alone does not demonstrate actual online behaviour. Use fictional examples and no personal information.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.learningObjective: State examples of upsetting content on the internet.
questions.prompt: Without describing anything frightening in detail, name two kinds of internet content that could upset a child.
questions.answer: Examples include frightening videos and hateful messages.
questions.explanation: Accept other age-appropriate examples of upsetting online material. Do not require the pupil to find or view any.

markingGuide.description: Names one suitable category.
Names a different suitable category.

questions.deliveryNote: Written understanding or planning precursor. This task alone does not demonstrate actual online behaviour. Use fictional examples and no personal information.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.learningObjective: State examples of upsetting content on the internet.
questions.prompt: Two cards describe online material: A is a polite explanation of a maths mistake; B mocks a group of people with hateful words. Identify the upsetting example and explain what makes it different from helpful correction.
questions.answer: B is upsetting because it attacks people. A offers polite help with a mistake.
questions.explanation: Disagreement or correction can be respectful; hateful treatment of people is different.

markingGuide.description: Identifies B and its hateful treatment.
Distinguishes polite correction of work from attacking people.

questions.deliveryNote: Written understanding or planning precursor. This task alone does not demonstrate actual online behaviour. Use fictional examples and no personal information.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.learningObjective: Report upsetting content to a teacher or parent.
questions.prompt: Role-play. Imagine a cartoon video unexpectedly becomes frightening. Your teacher plays a trusted adult. Show how you would stop watching and ask for help, saying what happened without repeating the frightening details.
questions.answer: The pupil stops watching or puts the device aside, tells the adult that a video was frightening and asks for help.
questions.explanation: Observe the reporting action. No frightening material is shown.

markingGuide.description: Stops the imagined viewing.
Tells the adult what kind of problem occurred.
Asks for help without replaying or sharing the content.

questions.deliveryNote: Teacher observes an offline role-play using only fictional, non-graphic material and a prepared mock interface where named. No live accounts, messages or personal information. Actual classroom delivery is unverified.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.learningObjective: Report upsetting content to a teacher or parent.
questions.prompt: Bola closes an upsetting page but is worried about it. Her parent is busy for a moment. What could she say when she can speak to the parent, and why should she still tell them even though the page is closed?
questions.answer: She could say, I saw something online that upset me and I need help. The adult can support her and help prevent another encounter.
questions.explanation: Closing a page does not remove the need for support. Accept a teacher or another trusted adult if the parent is unavailable.

markingGuide.description: Gives a clear request for help with the online experience.
Explains that the adult can offer support or help with future safety.

questions.deliveryNote: Written understanding or planning precursor. This task alone does not demonstrate actual online behaviour. Use fictional examples and no personal information.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.prompt: Role-play a class discussion on a pretend learning platform. A partner prefers a different story ending. Say one respectful reply that gives your view without insulting the partner, then let the partner respond.
questions.answer: For example: I prefer the ending where they share because it helps both friends. What do you think? The pupil listens to the response.
questions.explanation: Accept different relevant opinions. Assess respect and turn-taking, not agreement.

markingGuide.description: Expresses a relevant view politely.
Avoids personal insults and treats the partner respectfully.
Allows and listens to a response.

questions.deliveryNote: Teacher observes an offline role-play using only fictional, non-graphic material and a prepared mock interface where named. No live accounts, messages or personal information. Actual classroom delivery is unverified.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.prompt: A friend sends you a private photo of their drawing and asks you not to post it. You want to show the class online. Explain what you should do and why.
questions.answer: Do not post it against their wishes. Respect their privacy and ask permission before sharing; accept their refusal.
questions.explanation: Being able to copy a picture does not give permission to share it.

markingGuide.description: Does not post the picture against the friend's wishes.
Explains the need to respect privacy and permission.

questions.deliveryNote: Written understanding or planning precursor. This task alone does not demonstrate actual online behaviour. Use fictional examples and no personal information.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.prompt: Explain phishing in your own words using the idea of a message pretending to be from someone trusted.
questions.answer: Phishing is an attempt to trick someone through a deceptive message or communication, often pretending to be trusted, into revealing private information or taking an unsafe action.
questions.explanation: An attempt can be phishing even when the recipient does not fall for it.

markingGuide.description: Identifies an attempt to deceive through a message or communication.
Connects deception with obtaining private information or inducing unsafe action.

questions.deliveryNote: Written understanding or planning precursor. This task alone does not demonstrate actual online behaviour. Use fictional examples and no personal information.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.prompt: A pretend message claims to be from a learning club and asks for a secret login to claim a prize. Seyi refuses. Has refusing made the message stop being a phishing attempt? Explain.
questions.answer: No. It is still an attempt to use a false trusted identity or prize story to obtain secret information, even though Seyi did not provide it.
questions.explanation: Success is not required for an attempted deception to count as phishing.

markingGuide.description: Says it can still be a phishing attempt.
Explains the attempted deception to obtain secret information.

questions.deliveryNote: Written understanding or planning precursor. This task alone does not demonstrate actual online behaviour. Use fictional examples and no personal information.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.prompt: A message says your class account will close in five minutes unless you open an unexpected attachment. Identify two warning signs that mean you should stop and ask an adult.
questions.answer: The pressure to act within five minutes and the unexpected attachment are warning signs.
questions.explanation: These signs justify caution; the pupil should not open the attachment to investigate.

markingGuide.description: Identifies urgent pressure or threat.
Identifies the unexpected attachment.

questions.deliveryNote: Written understanding or planning precursor. This task alone does not demonstrate actual online behaviour. Use fictional examples and no personal information.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.prompt: An unexpected message uses the school badge and perfect spelling but asks you to send a secret login. Explain why the neat spelling and badge do not make it trustworthy.
questions.answer: A deceptive sender can copy a badge and write correctly. The unexpected request for a secret login is a reason to stop and check with the teacher.
questions.explanation: Poor spelling can be a warning, but correct spelling is not proof of trust.

markingGuide.description: Explains that appearance or correct spelling can be copied.
Identifies the secret-login request as a reason for caution.

questions.deliveryNote: Written understanding or planning precursor. This task alone does not demonstrate actual online behaviour. Use fictional examples and no personal information.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.prompt: Role-play with a paper message card: Free drawing kit! Send your private login now. Do not write a login. Show your teacher what you would do with this message and ask for help.
questions.answer: The pupil does not reply or follow any instruction, shows the card to the teacher and asks for help checking/reporting it.
questions.explanation: Use only the printed fictional card. No message is sent or secret collected.

markingGuide.description: Does not comply or reply.
Shows the message to the teacher.
Asks for help checking or reporting it.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.prompt: A suspicious message gives a phone number and says, Call this number to prove I am really your teacher. How should a pupil check the claim safely?
questions.answer: Ask the teacher in person or ask a trusted adult to use an already known school contact, rather than the number supplied by the suspicious message.
questions.explanation: A contact detail controlled by the sender cannot independently confirm the sender's identity.

markingGuide.description: Uses a trusted adult or independently known school contact.
Explains why the number in the suspicious message should not be relied on.

questions.deliveryNote: Written understanding or planning precursor. This task alone does not demonstrate actual online behaviour. Use fictional examples and no personal information.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.prompt: A pupil is repeatedly sent hurtful messages in an online game to make them feel ashamed. What is this behaviour called? Explain the part played by digital technology.
questions.answer: It is cyberbullying. Digital messages in the game are being used repeatedly to hurt or shame the pupil.
questions.explanation: The definition connects bullying behaviour with digital communication.

markingGuide.description: Names cyberbullying.
Links the repeated hurtful behaviour with the game's digital messages.

questions.deliveryNote: Written understanding or planning precursor. This task alone does not demonstrate actual online behaviour. Use fictional examples and no personal information.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.prompt: A player says, It cannot be bullying because I only sent the hurtful comments online, not in the classroom. Explain why that claim is wrong.
questions.answer: Bullying can happen through digital messages as well as face to face. Repeated online comments intended to hurt or shame someone can be cyberbullying.
questions.explanation: Online conduct can affect real people. A child can seek help with an upsetting incident even before repetition is established.

markingGuide.description: Recognises that online behaviour can be bullying.
Explains the repeated hurtful or shaming behaviour.

questions.deliveryNote: Written understanding or planning precursor. This task alone does not demonstrate actual online behaviour. Use fictional examples and no personal information.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.prompt: A person pretends to be another pupil in a class forum and posts mean messages under that pupil's name. Name this form of cyberbullying and explain the clue.
questions.answer: Impersonation. The person is using another pupil's identity to make others think that pupil wrote the messages.
questions.explanation: The identifying feature is pretending to be someone else.

markingGuide.description: Names impersonation.
Connects it to use of another pupil's identity.

questions.deliveryNote: Written understanding or planning precursor. This task alone does not demonstrate actual online behaviour. Use fictional examples and no personal information.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.prompt: Two fictional cases describe bullying online. In A, pupils repeatedly remove one child from a group to hurt them. In B, someone reveals another child's private information to embarrass them. Name the form shown in each case.
questions.answer: A is exclusion. B is outing, meaning harmful sharing of private information without permission.
questions.explanation: Accept descriptive names that accurately distinguish exclusion from exposing private information.

markingGuide.description: Identifies exclusion in A.
Identifies outing or non-consensual disclosure of private information in B.

questions.deliveryNote: Written understanding or planning precursor. This task alone does not demonstrate actual online behaviour. Use fictional examples and no personal information.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.learningObjective: Identify ways of dealing with cyberbullying.
questions.prompt: Your friend receives repeated mean messages. They ask you to send insults back for them. Give two helpful actions you could take instead, including one way to get help from a trusted adult.
questions.answer: Listen and offer to go with the friend to a trusted adult. Do not retaliate or spread the messages; help them get adult support with blocking/reporting if needed.
questions.explanation: Accept two distinct supportive actions, including adult-supported preservation of evidence. Do not require confrontation.

markingGuide.description: Gives one supportive action that does not retaliate.
Gives a different supportive action, with trusted-adult help included across the response.

questions.deliveryNote: Written understanding or planning precursor. This task alone does not demonstrate actual online behaviour. Use fictional examples and no personal information.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.learningObjective: Identify ways of dealing with cyberbullying.
questions.prompt: Role-play. Your teacher provides a harmless mock screen with a fictional sender, a Report button and a Block button. Point out the tools you could ask an adult to help use for repeated hurtful messages. Explain one reason to show the adult the message before removing it.
questions.answer: The pupil identifies Report and Block, asks for adult help and explains that the message may provide evidence of what happened.
questions.explanation: A mock screen is sufficient for this rehearsal, not evidence of operation on a real platform. Evidence is shown privately to a trusted adult, not reposted to peers.

markingGuide.description: Identifies both Report and Block.
Asks a trusted adult for help.
Explains that the message can provide evidence before removal.
